conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because mood changes are incredibly common in the first weeks and months postpartum.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and the care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer, and we can pause at any time.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

[soft sigh, eyes a bit downcast]

I… I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. Things that used to seem funny just feel kind of flat now. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday, and I forced a little smile because I didn’t want her to worry, but inside it felt like nothing. It’s like the joy got muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I gave a little chuckle when my husband tried to be funny, but it felt kind of forced. Mostly I just feel too tired or down to find things amusing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

I can’t say I’ve looked forward to much. When my friend texted about grabbing coffee next week, I agreed because I “should,” but I didn’t feel that little spark I used to. Even small things—like the show I used to love dropping new episodes—just seem like another task. I still do them, but the excitement isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up, voice cracks]

All the time. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not soothing him right. When he finally slept I just sat there crying, telling myself I’m already failing him. Even tiny stuff like spilling a little pumped milk makes me feel like I’m the worst mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap, voice tight]

Yeah… most of the day, honestly. I’ll just be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing, wondering if he’s breathing okay, or if that tiny cough means he’s getting sick. Sometimes I check the monitor ten times an hour. There’s this constant knot in my chest even when nothing’s wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. Last night I was washing bottles and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, my hands shook, and I had to sit on the floor until it passed. I kept thinking something awful was about to happen, even though everything was quiet. It’s scary when your body feels like it’s in danger but you can’t explain why.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]

Most days, yeah. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, the feedings, the pumping… it all piles up faster than I can handle it. I start one thing, the baby cries, and suddenly I’m standing in the middle of the mess trying not to cry myself. I keep telling myself millions of moms do this, but it still feels like I’m drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looks down, voice hoarse]

That’s been almost every night. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed, and my mind just keeps spinning—replaying everything I think I messed up, worrying about tomorrow, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. I’ll lie there for hours, drifting off around three, then snap awake at the slightest whimper over the monitor. I’m exhausted, but sleep feels impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes fill, nods slowly]

Pretty much all the time. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I see other moms posting happy pictures, and I wonder why I can’t feel that way. I love my baby—I do—but the sadness is just always there, sitting on my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[voice trembles, dabs eyes with sleeve]

Yes… it’s been almost every day this week. Sometimes it’s when the baby won’t latch, sometimes it’s just seeing a diaper commercial and feeling overwhelmed. I’ll hide in the bathroom so my partner doesn’t worry, but the tears just come. I feel so silly for crying over nothing, but I can’t stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never that. I get scared and overwhelmed, but I would never want to leave my baby. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom he deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Screening note – Postpartum visit

Presenting symptoms:
- Marked anhedonia (minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment)
- Persistent low mood with daily crying spells
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Generalized anxiety and sudden panic episodes (physical symptoms: chest tightness, trembling)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination
- Feeling overwhelmed and “drowning” in routine tasks

Pattern:
Consistent across all domains; symptoms present “pretty much all the time” and worsening over past week. No current suicidal ideation; explicitly endorses desire to remain alive for infant.

Screening significance:
High clinical concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features. No self-harm ideation reported; therefore no imminent safety risk per today’s assessment.

Risk factors documented:
- Daily sadness, anhedonia, worthlessness
- Mood-related insomnia
- Anxiety/panic attacks
- Functional impairment (difficulty completing chores, constant checking of monitor)

Plan:
Refer for immediate comprehensive depression/anxiety evaluation; safety plan reviewed; emergency resources provided.
